🗒️What This Means For You
  • Fed Hike: Since the 2026-09-16 Fed hike the Treasury-rate leg of IG returns is -1.25% (intraday, 7-year +18bp). At trading day 10 (last close) it was -1.68% against a five-campaign average of -0.36% at the same point — only 1994-95 was worse. Spreads have barely moved, so this is a rates story, not credit. The 10-year is +22bp since the hike vs a -1bp campaign average at the same point.
  • Stocks: US stocks closed slightly higher; Europe fell over 1%; Japan rose 3.3%.
  • FX: Major currencies barely moved; the dollar index rose 0.56%, which is unusual.
  • Technicals: US indexes sit far above their long-term trend, so they are stretched.
  • Sectors: Tech and energy led; real estate, financials and materials lagged this month.
  • Credit/Spreads: Lenders still ask very little extra yield, but European junk bonds weakened.
  • Crisis: Overall stress is moderate; the war and oil are the biggest risks.
  • Inflation: Core inflation trends are easing, but about 29% of prices rise fast.
  • Tech Bubble: Chip-stock prices and complacency look like 2000; broad valuations look less extreme.
  • Earnings & IPOs: Accenture beat estimates; Nike reports tonight; Oura and Anthropic lead IPOs.
  • Iran: US weighs strikes or talks; more troops are heading to the region.
  • Warsh: Warsh is focused on inflation; a rate hike this year is possible.
  • Week Ahead: Jobs report Friday, services survey Monday, Fed meeting minutes Wednesday.
  • Outlook: Near term neutral: falling yields help, while oil and war risk hurt.
  • Trades: Own energy as war insurance, keep high-yield bonds light, buy short Treasuries.
  • Trades Vol: 45 watchlist names screened: 1 buy, 2 sell, 21 hold long, 21 stay out
  • Treasury Liquidity: Treasury liquidity/rates-vol monitor: TLT 95/100 put skew +0.80 vol pts, Fed DKW real term premium +78bp.
  • 10Y Pattern: 10Y at 99th pctile, +4bp from the 2026 rim — still compressing, not a cup-and-handle.
  • Diesel Futures: Diesel: 1-9 of 10 signals point lower.
  • Bottom line: Calm US markets are underpricing oil and Fed hike risks. Stay selective.

The biggest story of the session was the oil shock. Brent crude jumped 5.32% to $103.25 and WTI rose 2.71% to $92.87, as the US weighed striking Iran against negotiating, and Washington sent its reply to Tehran's seven-day Hormuz proposal through Qatari mediators. Europe took the hit. The Euro Stoxx 50 fell 1.49%, the STOXX 600 fell 1.30% and the FTSE 100 fell 1.68%. Euro high-yield spreads also widened 18bps to 3.39%. Wall Street held up because Treasury yields fell back from multiyear highs: the US 2Y dropped 9.56bps to 4.7914% and the 10Y fell 4.42bps to 5.2407%. The S&P 500 gained 0.19% to 7666.45, the Russell 2000 0.35% and the Dow 0.04%, while the VIX was nearly unchanged at 16.39. In Japan, the Nikkei surged 3.30% even as the JGB 10Y rose 6bps to 3.125%. Versus the prior session, sentiment split by region: the US stayed calm, Europe moved toward risk-off and energy was bid everywhere. Two big tests come next: Nike's results after the close and Friday's September payrolls.

“Brent is above $100, Europe is bleeding and the VIX is at 16. America is drinking its coffee like nothing is brewing in the Gulf.”
📊Markets

US: the S&P 500 rose 0.19% (+14.91) to 7666.45, the Nasdaq Composite 0.04% to 26871.6, the Dow 0.04% to 50926.56 and the Russell 2000 0.35% to 2806.625. The VIX was nearly flat at 16.39 (+0.05). Europe sold off on the oil and war headlines: the Euro Stoxx 50 fell 1.49% to 6175.45, the STOXX 600 1.30% to 626.65 and the FTSE 100 1.68% to 10428.27. The Nikkei 225 was the outlier, up 3.30% (+2203.0) to 68956.72. Rates rallied outside Japan. The US 2Y fell 9.56bps to 4.7914%, the 10Y 4.42bps to 5.2407% and the 30Y 1.6bps to 5.6126%, so the curve steepened. The Bund 10Y fell 7.8bps to 3.508% and the Gilt 10Y 2.6bps to 5.398%, but the JGB 10Y rose 6bps to 3.125%. Commodities: Brent rose 5.32% to 103.25, WTI 2.71% to 92.87 and silver 0.94%, while gold was nearly flat at 4179.85 (+0.05%). Copper fell 1.26% and nat gas 1.95%.

NY Harbor ULSD (US Diesel) — current: 464.20 cents/gal vs WTI

NY Harbor ULSD is at 464.2 cents/gal, near the top of its history on every gauge: outright price, crack spread and the front of the curve all sit at roughly the 98.5th–99.8th percentile. The crack spread at 102.094 $/bbl (z 5.61) and a front-minus-12th spread of 114.15 cents/gal (z 5.19) show a very tight prompt diesel market. The curve falls steeply from 464.2 in month 1 to 350.05 by month 12 and 271.24 by month 36. History favours a pullback from this kind of extreme, but every stop is far from entry, so timing and position size matter more than direction.

ICE Low Sulphur Gasoil (Europe/Asia Diesel) — current: 1447.75 $/tonne vs Brent

ICE Low Sulphur Gasoil is trading at 1447.75 $/tonne, a 99.8th-percentile level. The curve is in steep backwardation, falling to 1012.0 by month 12 and 759.5 by month 36, which points to an acute shortage of prompt diesel rather than a broad repricing along the whole curve. Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

🔄Sector Analysis

US: the 1-day leaders were Energy (+1.92%), Industrials (+1.00%), Info Tech (+0.76%) and Utilities (+0.61%). Health Care (-1.30%) and Comm Services (-1.19%) lagged. The 1-month window reads as growth and inflation hedges against everything else. Info Tech (+6.28%) and Comm Services (+3.57%) are the only gainers. Rate-sensitive and defensive groups are worst: Real Estate -7.18%, Utilities -6.36%, Financials -6.31%, Materials -6.07%, Cons Discr -4.24% and Cons Staples -4.03%. YTD, Energy (+37.20%) and Info Tech (+28.76%) dominate, while Utilities (-8.17%), Cons Discr (-5.35%) and Financials (-2.59%) trail. Global sectors tell the same story, with Info Tech +6.44% over 1m and +36.18% YTD and Energy +31.75% YTD. Global Materials (-8.25% 1m) and Financials (-1.13% 1d, -6.23% 1m) are weaker than their US peers, which matches Europe's selloff. The market is concentrated: it is paying for AI-tech and energy, the two sectors that do well with higher yields and oil, and selling bond proxies and the consumer.

🧮Fixed Income Spreadscomputed

Computed: US IG OAS is 0.80% (z -0.80, 6th percentile). Historically that is near the tight end, with a minimum of 0.71% and a maximum of 6.18%, and it sits at 0% of each crisis peak (GFC, EuroDebt, COVID, 2022 hikes). US HY OAS is 3.11% (z -0.72, 19th percentile) and is 7% of the way toward the 2022-hike stress level. Europe is where today's damage showed. EUR HY OAS widened 18bps to 3.39% (z -0.53, 29th percentile; 12% of COVID, 7% of 2022) and EUR IG widened 4bps to 0.95% (25th percentile; 12% of COVID). EM USD OAS was unchanged at 1.70% (z -1.29, 6th percentile). Key levels: US IG at 0.71% is the historical floor. Getting there would take falling yields plus a ceasefire. A move to 1.00–1.20% would need Brent holding above $100 together with a Fed hike that tightens financial conditions. US HY at 2.33% is the historical tight and would need a soft landing with lower oil. A move to 4.00%+ would take an energy-led growth scare or equity drawdown. EUR HY above 3.75% would signal that the European oil shock is spreading into credit.

Widening velocity, not level. Near an all-time high a 63d widening past the trigger has historically raised P(SPX -10% within 3m) from ~8.6% to ~21.9% (Baa p=0.013, HY p=0.028, IG p=0.047, 1990-2026, corroborated on three independently-sourced series). The spread LEVEL carries no such signal once you control for already being in a drawdown (p=0.562) — tight spreads near a high are expected and are not reassurance. ARMED marks elevated tail RISK, not a sell: 78% of past ARMED episodes did not produce a 10% drawdown. This rule failed all three pre-registered gates as a tradable overlay (placebo p=0.465); do not size positions off it. See the monitor_spread skill (MONITOR_SPREAD.md).

💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 48th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +78bp.

Latest reading is +0.80 vol points (38th percentile of the 32 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.51 (48th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), deteriorating over the past 3 months (+0.05 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.49pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +78bp (90th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 10bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +11bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 108.1 (78th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 115bp (steeper by 43bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

Recreates 5 charts from Bloomberg MacroScope, 'Treasury Market Liquidity Is a Live Issue Again' (Simon White, 19-Aug-2026). TLT skew accumulates one point per report run -- Bloomberg's option-surface field is snapshot-only, not retrievable historically via the API. Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Cup test

COMPONENTLEVELDATE
Left rim6.79%2000-01-20
Cup base0.51%2020-08-04
Right rim5.28%2026-09-30

Retracement of the left-rim decline: 76% (needs ≥90% to pass). 10Y level that passes: 6.16% (92bp above today).
Retracement = (right rim − cup base) / (left rim − cup base) = (5.28 − 0.51) / (6.79 − 0.51) = 76%.
Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base) = 0.51 + 0.90 × (6.79 − 0.51) = 6.16%.

Same test on each trailing window: cup base = lowest close in the window, left rim = highest close before it, right rim = highest close after it. Cup complete at ≥90% retracement; above 110% the yield has run past the old high (a breakout, not a cup). No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

🗞️Street View — Where the Cycle Is HeadingCURATED · AS OF 2026-10-01

Consensus is a short, shallow campaign: one or two more 25bp hikes, December more likely than October. The debate is whether hiking into an energy shock ends in recession, and the bond market is already doing some of the tightening.

The Fed

  • Sept 16: unanimous 25bp hike to 3.75–4.00%, the first since 2023. Dots: median one more hike in 2026; 16 of 18 see at least one, 4 see two. Inflation not back at 2% until 2029. (CNBC, FedAndMarkets)
  • Warsh's message was distinctly hawkish (inflation 'too high and broad-based'); the Conference Board calls it 'not a one and done'. (Conference Board)
  • Sept 29, Williams (NY Fed): 'no need for urgency'; one more hike 'late this year' may be appropriate; the biggest inflation shocks have passed. (Bloomberg, NY Fed)
  • Sept 30, August PCE came in soft: headline 3.4% (vs 3.7% expected), core 3.0% (vs 3.3%). October odds fell; December still priced. Kashkari: inflation 'still too high'. (CNBC, CNBC (Kashkari))

Market pricing

  • October 28 hike odds vary widely by venue, roughly 35% to 69% (prediction markets highest, CME futures ~58%), mostly measured before the soft PCE print. (PredictionMarketsPicks)
  • About 83% odds of another hike by year-end; futures price ~93bp of tightening over the next 9 meetings, more than the dots. (Forbes)

Bonds and credit

  • 10-year Treasury above 5.25% (Sept 28), the highest since 2007; 30-year ~5.49%. Drivers cited: sticky energy inflation (Iran war), heavy issuance, AI capex demand. Term premium ~1.0–1.4%. (CNBC, CNBC (Warsh's yield problem))
  • AI-related issuers trade ~115bp vs ~78bp for IG overall; high-yield AI supply $40B year to date vs $12B in all of 2025. BNP and Goldman warn the issuance could pressure spreads. (Reuters, Bloomberg (BNP))

The bear case

  • Rosenberg: the Fed has never hiked into an energy shock without a recession, and AI won't save it this time. (TheStreet)
  • Goldman called the case for hiking 'weak' (demand not overheating, energy inflation should fade when the war ends). Oxford Economics: 'The Fed cannot control energy prices'; the risk is a weaker labor market. (CNN)

Read-through: For bonds, the bigger risk is the long end, not the Fed: term premium and supply keeping the 10-year above 5% matter more than one extra 25bp. The recession call is loud but isn't in any sell-side house view yet.

Curated summary of published Fed, market and economist commentary (news and research via the web), not a computed series and not a forecast. Odds differ by venue and move daily.

🔥Is Inflation Persistent?

Persistence score: 55/100 — Moderately persistent. Underlying trend measures are drifting lower, but a fat tail of fast-rising prices plus an oil shock keep the Fed from declaring victory. The computed Core-Trend Sub-Score sits mid-to-upper range, and every tracked trend measure is marked 'falling'. Against that, the Dallas Fed breadth data shows 28.9% of the PCE basket rising faster than 5% (13.2% above 10% and 15.7% at 5-10%), while 25.8% is falling. The distribution is splitting in two rather than settling at target. Core PCE at 3.00759% YoY is well above Core CPI at 2.4%, which keeps the Fed's preferred gauge uncomfortable. Brent above $100 threatens the 1y breakeven (already 2.8023%) more than the 5y (2.3832%).

Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle

Valuation marker: today's Nasdaq P/E (39x) ≈ 22% of the ~175x 2000-peak P/E.

IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

The computed dashboard says the danger lies in the wiring, not in headline valuations. A Nasdaq at 38.73x trailing earnings is nowhere near the 175x of 2000, and the current cycle (anchored Oct-2022 at 100) has reached 244.6 after 48 months. On the 1990-anchor path, the dot-com run did not peak until month 113. What rhymes with 2000 is leadership concentration in semis, credit spreads tighter than at the 2000 top, and a VIX and financial-conditions index that signal more complacency than then. What does not rhyme: retail sentiment is net bearish, consumer confidence is low, the curve is positively sloped and PMIs have not rolled over. My analyst estimates, which I did not web-verify this run, put top-10 S&P concentration near 40%, CAPE around 39x and market-cap/GDP near 215%. Those are 2000-like or worse on broad measures, which argues the froth has migrated from multiples into concentration. IPO froth (analyst estimate 60) is building: Cerebras debuted as 2026's largest IPO, Oura is pricing about $2.2B and Anthropic targets a late-October Nasdaq listing at a reported valuation as high as $2 trillion. A mega-cap AI IPO wave is the classic late-stage supply signal to watch.

⚔️Iran War

Day 216 of the conflict (GlobalSecurity, Oct 1, 2026). President Trump said the US would decide 'very soon' whether to strike Iran or negotiate. Iran received Washington's response to its seven-day Hormuz proposal through Qatari mediators. Reporting indicates the two sides largely agree on the steps toward a ceasefire but disagree on their order (CBS News live updates). Secretary of State Rubio demanded that Iran's UN General Assembly delegation leave the US after talks stalled. Trump said he doesn't think 'you could ever have peace' with Iran and renewed his threat to resume attacks after the midterms. Three ships carrying over 7,000 sailors and 2,000 Marines are heading to the Middle East. UK PM Andy Burnham said the UK government believes Iran played a role in the RAF Fairford incident. Netanyahu said it is too early to say whether Iran was involved in a passenger-jet co-pilot incident under investigation in Saudi Arabia (Jerusalem Post live, Just Security Early Edition, Oct 1, 2026). Market read (analyst): the Brent +5.32% move prices a higher chance of escalation around Hormuz. A sequencing deal via Qatar is the main downside risk for oil.

🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

Inferred: hold at the next meeting with a hawkish bias and a real chance of a 25bp hike. Warsh said at Jackson Hole that the Fed must be 'confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective clearly and at sufficient speed. Otherwise, we have work to do.' Core PCE at 3.00759% and Brent above $100 fail that test. One chief economist read it as a hike 'by October or December.' I have not verified the next FOMC date in this run.

~1 YEAR

Inferred: one or two 25bp hikes from the current 3.50–3.75% range over the next year, unless underlying inflation measures keep falling. Then a pause. Also less forward guidance and a 'quieter' Fed that avoids quasi-commitments, which means more policy uncertainty and higher rate volatility. The 2Y at 4.7914%, well above the funds range, shows the market already leans this way.

Warsh became chair in May 2026 and held rates at 3.50–3.75% at his first FOMC. At Jackson Hole (Aug 28, 2026) he said the economy 'appears to have strengthened' but put the focus squarely on prices. He also rejected quasi-commitments on rates, saying they 'inhibit our own freedom to make the right calls.' The hawkish lean and lack of guidance are on record. The hike timing is my inference from those statements and today's data, not something Warsh has said.

Sources: Keynote remarks by Chairman Warsh at the 2026 Jackson Hole Economic Policy Symposium (Federal Reserve Board) · Fed Chairman Warsh expresses concern about inflation, advocates for 'quieter' central bank (CNBC) · Fed will have 'work to do' if inflation doesn't fade, Warsh says (CBS News) · What Warsh's Jackson Hole speech signals about where interest rates are headed (Fox Business)
